bib.title: LLM Post-Training: A Deep Dive into Reasoning Large Language Models

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "LLM Post-Training: A Deep Dive into Reasoning Large Language Models", Komal Kumar, Tajamul Ashraf, Omkar Thawakar, Rao Muhammad Anwer, Hisham Cholakkal, Mubarak Shah, Ming-Hsuan Yang, Phillip H.S. Torr, Fahad Shahbaz Khan, Salman Khan. arXiv:2502.21321v2 [cs.CL], 24 Mar 2025. Preprint (survey and tutorial).

COVERAGE: All 32 pages. I read 199,317 chars of body text with no sampling. Pages 1-23 are body (about 2,640 lines); pages 23-32 are the reference list, which I skimmed for origins only. The text extracted cleanly. Equations are partly mangled but readable.

CLAIMS (ranked)
- claim: LLM generation is framed as an MDP (state = tokens so far, action = next token, reward R(s,a)). RL optimises expected return, where MLE optimises likelihood on static data.
  number: none
  setup: background, Sec 2
  quote: "the state st represents the sequence of tokens generated so far, the action at is the next token, and a reward R(st,at) evaluates the quality of the output."
  where: p3

- claim: RL for LLMs differs from classic RL in four ways: a huge action space, sparse and delayed feedback, hard credit assignment, and several objectives at once.
  number: none
  setup: intro, p2
  quote: "Instead of a finite action set, LLMs select tokens from a vast vocabulary, and their evolving state comprises an ever-growing text sequence ... Feedback in language-based RL is also sparse [77], subjective, and delayed"
  where: p2

- claim: The standard RLHF pipeline is SFT, then reward-model training on human preferences, then PPO against the reward model. The survey lists "reward modeling and alignment" as a fourth step.
  number: none
  setup: Sec 3 and 3.2.3
  quote: "Third, PPO is employed in the RLHF [58] pipeline by using human-provided preference scores (or rankings) to shape R and thereby guide the policy updates."
  where: p5, p9

- claim: Reward models are trained with a Bradley-Terry pairwise loss or a Plackett-Luce ranking loss. The reward model learns relative preferences, not calibrated scores.
  number: none
  setup: Sec 3.1
  quote: "The reward model learns relative preferences rather than absolute scores. This avoids the need for calibrated human ratings and focuses on pairwise comparisons."
  where: p6, p8

- claim: Outcome reward models (ORM) are simple but give a credit-assignment problem on long responses. Process reward models (PRM) score steps but need costlier annotation. The two can be combined.
  number: none
  setup: Sec 3.1.3-3.1.4
  quote: "For long-response tasks, outcome based reward can lead to credit assignment problem" and "Process rewards can be combined with outcome rewards for a strong multi-phase training signal."
  where: p7

- claim: PPO uses a clipped probability-ratio objective with GAE advantages from a learned value function. A KL penalty to the base model (-beta*KL) guards against reward hacking.
  number: none
  setup: Sec 3.2.2
  quote: "The KL term KL(π∥ρ) prevents over-optimization to the proxy reward r(x,y) (i.e., reward hacking)."
  where: p8-9

- claim: GRPO drops the critic. It samples G outputs per question and normalises rewards within the group, (r - mean)/std, as the advantage. It keeps PPO-style clipping and a KL term to the reference model. It has an outcome mode (one reward for all tokens) and a process mode (sum of later step rewards).
  number: none
  setup: Sec 3.2.8, DeepSeekMath/R1 lineage
  quote: "GRPO ... removes the need for a separate value model (critic model) and instead estimates the baseline reward from a group of sampled LLM outputs. This significantly reduces memory usage and stabilizes policy learning."
  where: p10-11

- claim: DPO optimises a preference loss on log-probability ratios against a reference policy, with no reward model, critic or RL loop. The survey says it loses per-step credit assignment.
  number: none
  setup: Sec 3.2.6, Fig 3 compares PPO, GRPO and DPO
  quote: "This granularity is lost in DPO, which treats entire trajectories uniformly."
  where: p9-10

- claim: DeepSeek-R1-Zero is RL only, with no SFT. DeepSeek-R1 uses cold-start data, then reasoning RL with GRPO and rule-based rewards, then rejection sampling and SFT, then a second RL stage for alignment, then distillation to Qwen and Llama models of 1.5B to 70B.
  number: ~800k mixed SFT samples; cold start "thousands" of samples
  setup: Sec 3.3, taken from Guo et al. 2025
  quote: "DeepSeek-R1-Zero operates with a purely Reinforcement Learning approach, excluding any SFT." and "(often around 800k samples)"
  where: p11-12

- claim: Beam search beats best-of-N at low compute on hard questions. Best-of-N scales better on easy ones. Best-of-N can approach RLHF when the reward model is strong, but it is vulnerable to reward hacking if the proxy is imperfect.
  number: none
  setup: Sec 5.1-5.2, drawn from Snell et al. and Gao et al.
  quote: "Beam search (effective for harder questions) outperforms best-of-N sampling at low compute budgets, while best-of-N scales better for easier tasks."
  where: p14-15

- claim: Compute-optimal test-time scaling (Snell et al.) sorts prompts into five difficulty levels. Easy prompts get sequential revision, and hard prompts get parallel sampling or beam search. It matches best-of-N with about a quarter of the compute.
  number: 4x less compute
  setup: five difficulty bins; difficulty from oracle success rate or verifier score
  quote: "this method achieves four times lower compute usage than traditional best-of-N sampling while maintaining equivalent performance."
  where: p15

- claim: Test-time compute on a small model can match a much larger model on easy and intermediate problems. Pretraining stays better on the hardest tasks.
  number: 14x larger model; 4x fewer FLOPs
  setup: MATH-style benchmarks; limited inference tokens, self-improvement setting; cites Snell et al. [268]
  quote: "TTS achieves results comparable to a model 14 × larger on easy to intermediate tasks (e.g., MATH benchmarks), while reducing inference costs by 4 × fewer FLOPs in compute-intensive scenarios [268]. However, pretraining remains superior for the hardest tasks"
  where: p19

- claim: Pure RL on LLMs is expensive and often loses to distillation. Distilled models often beat RL-trained ones at lower training cost.
  number: none
  setup: future-directions section
  quote: "Current RL methods for LLMs require prohibitive computational resources [352] while often underperforming knowledge distillation techniques [93]."
  where: p22

- claim: Reward misgeneralisation and sparse terminal rewards are open problems in multi-step reasoning. The survey says DPO needs pairwise data and cannot use failure trajectories well.
  number: none
  setup: future-directions section
  quote: "Current RL approaches suffer from reward misgeneralization, where models over-optimize superficial proxy metrics rather than genuine reasoning quality."
  where: p22

- claim: Overthinking (excessively long reasoning chains) wastes compute. The survey proposes partial rollouts, length penalties and long-to-short distillation. The figure below has no stated setup and I could not verify it.
  number: 22% wasted computation
  setup: none given in text
  quote: "Overthinking Phenomenon: Analysis reveals 22% wasted computation is in reasoning chains exceeding optimal reasoning length."
  where: p22

- claim: Other survey figures come with no setup in the text, so treat them as weak. They are: PRM-guided tree search with online distillation reaching 4x efficiency and 94% on MATH; confidence estimators adding ~18% latency; catastrophic forgetting costing 29% of base capability during RL fine-tuning; MMLU correlating poorly (r=0.34) with real-world performance; and small models reaching o1-level accuracy in 32 rollouts with particle-based Monte Carlo (4-16x scaling efficiency; the citation is printed as "[? ]").
  number: 94%, 18%, 29%, r=0.34, 32 rollouts, 4-16x
  setup: unspecified in the survey
  quote: "maintaining 94% solution accuracy on MATH dataset." / "the small models achieved o1 level accuracy in only 32 rollouts, a 4–16x improvement in scaling efficiency" / "catastrophic forgetting rresults in a degradation of 29% of base capabilities during RL fine-tuning [374]" / "MMLU scores correlating poorly (r = 0.34) with real-world performance [375]"
  where: p22-23

- claim: Satori trains in two stages. Stage 1 is format tuning on 10K synthetic trajectories. Stage 2 is PPO self-improvement with a Restart and Explore strategy.
  number: 10K trajectories
  setup: Sec 5.12, citing Shen et al. [260]
  quote: "a large set of 10K synthetic trajectories generated by a multi-agent framework"
  where: p18

- claim: Self-consistency samples several chain-of-thought paths and takes the majority answer. It needs no new training. Tree-of-Thoughts and Graph-of-Thoughts are search over thoughts.
  number: none (example of 20 CoTs)
  setup: Sec 5.4-5.7
  quote: "one might sample, e.g., 20 CoTs for a math problem and see what final answer appears most frequently"
  where: p15-17

- claim: OREO is an offline RL method that uses sparse outcome rewards and a soft-Bellman value function. It enables value-guided beam search. TRPO uses a hard KL constraint and second-order optimisation, so PPO is preferred in practice.
  number: none
  setup: Sec 3.2.5 and 3.2.7
  quote: "In practice, PPO is preferred over TRPO due to its simplicity, ease of implementation, and comparable performance in large-scale applications like RLHF."
  where: p9-10

- claim: RLAIF replaces human labels with AI-generated preference labels. The survey calls it scalable but warns of echo-chamber bias.
  number: none
  setup: Sec 3.2.4 and 7
  quote: "Empirical studies indicate that RLAIF [95, 170] is a scalable and efficient alternative to RLHF"
  where: p9, p21

LIMITS
- The survey cites other work and runs no experiments of its own. Many numbers are attached to a citation and nothing else, with no model, dataset or scale stated.
- The authors concede these open problems: reward hacking and misgeneralisation, credit assignment, catastrophic forgetting, human-feedback cost, how much test-time compute is enough, the overthinking phenomenon, and privacy.
- The authors write "Reasoning" to mean "statistical patterns in data rather than explicit logical inference."
- It is dated early 2025. It covers R1, o1/o3 and Kimi K1.5 only at a high level. Later work on GRPO variants and RLVR (the later refinements of the method) is absent.
- Table 1 (about 45 models with RL methods, size and TTS flags) has questionable rows, for example "Zed 500B", "Supernova", "Phi-4 28B/70B/140B" and "Chinchilla RLHF, PPO". Do not cite it.

BUILDS ON: Ouyang 2022 (InstructGPT/RLHF); Schulman 2017 (PPO); Schulman 2017 (TRPO); Schulman 2018 (GAE); Rafailov 2023 (DPO); Shao 2024 (DeepSeekMath, GRPO); Guo 2025 (DeepSeek-R1); Lee 2023 (RLAIF); Bai 2022 (Constitutional AI); Snell 2024 (test-time compute); Gao 2023 (reward overoptimisation); Wei 2022 (CoT); Wang 2022 (self-consistency); Yao 2023 (ToT); Nakano 2021 (WebGPT); Ranzato 2016 (MIXER); SCST; Coulom 2006 (MCTS).

CODE: none. The survey is math-only. The core formulas as printed are:
- PPO: "LPPO(θ) = Et[min(rt(θ)At, clip(rt(θ), 1−ϵ, 1+ϵ)At)]" (p8)
- GRPO advantage: "¯ri = (ri − mean(r)) / std(r)" (p10-11)
- KL-penalised objective: "J(π) = E[r(x,y) − β KL(π(·|x)∥ρ(·|x))]" (p9)

FIGURES
- Fig 1 (p1): taxonomy of post-training into fine-tuning, RL and test-time scaling.
- Fig 3 (p10): PPO vs GRPO vs DPO block comparison. It shows which approach needs a value model, a reference model or a group computation, and it is the fastest way to see the differences. The caption is "Comparison of PPO [73], GRPO [59], and DPO [162]."
- Fig 5 (p14): test-time scaling taxonomy.
- Fig 6 (p16): CoT, self-consistency, ToT and GoT compared.
- Fig 7 (p21): yearly trend plots. They are bibliometric, so low value.
- I did not run the figures script because the captions were in the text. I did not view the images.

PROBLEMS
- I found no embedded instructions in the PDF.
- Citation errors:
  - Ref [162] for DPO is actually Guo et al., "Direct language model alignment from online AI feedback"; the DPO paper is [57].
  - REINFORCE is cited to [114], a bandit NMT paper, and [115], a garbled law-book entry.
  - "Policy Reward Modeling (PRM)" on p7 is a naming slip for process reward model.
- Section 3.2.1 "ORPO" is described as a Bradley-Terry odds loss with no SFT term, which is not the ORPO paper's formulation. Do not use it as a source on ORPO.
- The DPO loss as printed is missing the log and the minus sign.
- There is a cross-reference error: "As described in Sec. 5.4, CoT format data..." (p15).
- Several extracted formulas have fractions broken across lines, but they are recoverable.
